title: The SPAN Story
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
In policy meetings, the chairs are always counted, but youth voices rarely are. That’s what sparked the founding of SPAN, Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide, in March 2025, what began as a handful of students has grown into a national youth-led coalition with real legislative impact. In just a few months, SPAN has helped shape 15 pieces of healthcare legislation across four states, proving that student voices don’t just belong in the conversation; they move it forward.

SPAN is a student-powered policy organization working to make healthcare more patient-centered, equitable, and accessible. We train high school and college students to write policy memos, deliver public testimony, and meet with lawmakers. Our students fight for reforms that directly affect their communities — from expanding mental health access in schools to increasing transparency in hospitals. Our initiatives are entirely youth-run, supported by a national team that provides legal, legislative, and research support to help students turn their ideas into action.

At SPAN, we don’t treat advocacy as a future goal. We treat it as a responsibility now. At SPAN, we don’t wait to be given influence. We earn it. Through research, advocacy, and action, our students are stepping into policy spaces and leaving a mark.

Because when young people are not just present but heard, we don’t just count the chairs in the room: we reshape the room entirely.

Learn more at spanationwide.org.

  • Written by Ashita Virani, Editorial & Business Lead at SPAN.

title: AI in Healthcare: Transforming Diagnosis, Documentation, and Patient Monitoring
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
Artificial Intelligence

Healthcare

Diagnosis

Patients

Advocacy

When a patient walks into a clinic today, the first observer might not be a doctor. It could be an algorithm. Artificial intelligence (AI) has quietly become the unseen assistant in hospitals and clinics around the world, helping physicians diagnose diseases, document visits, and monitor patients with a level of precision once thought impossible. What was once an ambitious idea at the intersection of technology and medicine is now an integral part of modern care.

AI in Diagnosis

AI’s most visible impact lies in diagnosis. Machine learning models trained on thousands of medical images can now detect conditions ranging from cancer to pneumonia with remarkable accuracy. Tools such as Google’s DeepMind and Aidoc help radiologists interpret scans faster, flagging subtle abnormalities that may escape even trained eyes. In dermatology, AI can distinguish between benign and malignant skin lesions in seconds, while in cardiology, predictive models assess the risk of heart disease long before symptoms appear.

These systems do not replace human judgment; they refine it. By handling repetitive analysis and providing data-driven insights, AI allows clinicians to focus on empathy, interpretation, and treatment, reinforcing the human core of healthcare rather than removing it.

AI in Documentation

Beyond diagnosis, AI is transforming the less glamorous but equally essential realm of medical documentation. Tools like Nuance’s Dragon Medical One and Suki AI use natural language processing (NLP) to transcribe and organize physician-patient conversations into detailed medical notes. This automation reduces the hours physicians spend typing, minimizing burnout and freeing up time for patient care.

AI in Patient Monitoring

Perhaps the most personal role of AI appears in patient monitoring. Wearable devices powered by AI track vital signs such as heart rate, oxygen levels, and sleep cycles, creating a continuous stream of data that physicians can interpret remotely. Systems like Biofourmis and Current Health even predict medical emergencies such as sepsis or heart failure before they occur, prompting earlier intervention.

This predictive monitoring represents a profound shift from reactive medicine to proactive prevention. For patients with chronic illnesses, AI does not just observe. It listens, learns, and alerts, providing reassurance that help is available before crisis strikes.

Challenges and Ethics

Still, the path forward demands caution. AI models can inherit biases from their data, raising ethical concerns about fairness and accuracy. Privacy, transparency, and accountability must remain central to AI development. The challenge is not only to create smarter algorithms but also to build trust between humans and machines, ensuring technology complements compassion rather than competes with it.

Conclusion

When a patient walks into a clinic tomorrow, AI will again be there, analyzing, documenting, and monitoring with quiet precision. Yet the true promise of this technology is not in replacing the doctor’s intuition; it is in amplifying it. AI’s strength lies in partnership, not supremacy. As healthcare continues to evolve, the goal remains unchanged: to heal with both intelligence and humanity. In this full circle, AI becomes what it was always meant to be, not a machine that replaces care but one that helps us care better.

  • Written by Ashita Virani, Editorial & Business Lead at SPAN.

title: Do Physician-Owned Hospitals Deserve a Second Look?
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
Physician-owned hospitals (POHs) have sparked a long-standing debate about the balance of cost, quality, and ethics of POHs within the U.S. healthcare system. Supporters of POHs argue that physician ownership encourages innovation, efficiency, higher-quality, and more patient-centered care. On the other hand, critics of POHs highlight the possibility for scrupulous business practices, such as self-referral, overutilization, and selective treatment of healthier, more profitable patients, also known as cherry-picking. These concerns led to calls for federal intervention, most notably the Affordable Care Act’s restrictions on POHs, which prevented their expansion despite the fact that multiple studies supporting that they deliver equal or superior cost efficiency and care quality. As healthcare policymakers continue to search for methods to improve the industry without sacrificing equality to cherry-picking or ease of access to all patients. As healthcare policymakers continue to search for methods to improve the industry without sacrificing equality to cherry-picking or ease of access to all patients, the controversy surrounding POHs patient benefits and discrimination raises a crucial question: should POHs remain under strict legislative restrictions, or should modern policymakers re-evaluate the role of POHs within the healthcare system?

History

Concerns about physician self-referral and conflicts of interest, particularly that physician ownership might lead to overuse, “cherry picking” of healthier patients with better insurance, and leave community hospitals with sicker, unprofitable patients, led Congress to gradually limit the number of physician-owned hospitals in a series of legislation culminating in Section 6001 of the Affordable Care Act (2010), which effectively prohibited the construction of new POHs and significantly curbed any further growth of existing ones as a condition of Medicare program participation. These restrictions built on earlier efforts like the Stark Law and the 2003 Medicare moratorium, reflecting long-standing fears that financial incentives could distort clinical decision-making and threaten the financial stability of full-service community and rural hospitals. However, in the years since, studies and policy evaluations, such as those related to the Ways & Means-associated manuscript, have raised doubts about the content of such concerns, noting that POHs appear to provide equivalent, if not better, quality of care at significantly lower cost to Medicare. Consequently, future policy has increasingly turned to an easing of restrictions imposed by ACA legislation, particularly in rural regions, while still proposing allowance for the growth of POHs, though under a watchful eye, to ensure that no potentially questionable ethics are involved.

Benefits

POHs have been shown in multiple cases to offer substantial cost savings when it comes to Medicare, particularly for especially expensive visits. A paper by UConn Health and Loyola University Chicago found that POHs could save Medicare over $1.1 billion annually on the total cost of care across 20 of the most expensive conditions, with cost reductions ranging from 8.6% to 15.2% compared with other hospitals in the same region. Critics would argue that these cost benefits could have come from cherry-picking healthier patients who are more profitable, but researchers found that patients treated at POHs had similar demographic and health history profiles. These researchers went on to mention that physician ownership often leads to better aligned management that keeps clinical decision-making in mind, reducing unnecessary utilization, streamlining care paths, and promoting a more efficient use of hospital resources. By promoting accountability and focusing on value-driven care, well-structured POHs can contribute to a more cost-effective healthcare system without sacrificing quality, access, or fairness in patient treatment, cementing them as a major resource for creating a better healthcare system.

Risks

However, some analyses from organizations like the American Hospital Association emphasize risks associated with expanding POHs, particularly in rural and underserved areas. In these areas, hospitals focused on comprehensive care and available 24/7 are crucial as these hospitals may be the only ones for miles. Studies have repeatedly found that some POHs tend to focus on a narrower range of specialized services, treat a healthier, commercially insured patient mix, and provide fewer emergency and high-acuity services than full-service community hospitals, which can shift costly emergency care burdens onto other providers, and in the worst case, make emergency care inaccessible due to transport time and overcapacity. Moreover, modeling analyses suggest that the entrance of a POH into the same market as a sole community hospital could significantly reduce the community hospital’s financial margins, potentially jeopardizing its ability to sustain essential services, retain staff, and remain open; this competition may appear to encourage higher quality care, but in reality, it often drains resources and puts unnecessary stress on an already high-tension environment. These concerns underscore the importance of crafting policy that preserves access while exploring the cost-efficiency benefits POHs may offer.

Conclusion

Overall, the debate concerning POHs is an argument about ethics and efficiency. Although concerns about encroaching on pre-existing hospitals, self-referral, and cherry-picking greatly warrant oversight, there is plenty of evidence to suggest that POHs can deliver high-quality care at lower cost, especially for common and expensive conditions, without compromising quality of care. Instead of broad restrictions out of fear-mongering, policymakers should pursue a more balanced approach that allows carefully regulated POHs to operate alongside community hospitals, with specific legislation to protect emergency access and scarce rural areas. In a modern-day America that values high-quality care along with reducing the heavily taxing cost of healthcare, physician-owned hospitals do not represent a threat to the healthcare system, but a potential solution to improve efficiency, accountability, and patient-centered care when watched carefully.

title: The GLP-1 Drug Revolution
author: Students for Patient Advocacy Nationwide
description:
One of the main spectacles of the Super Bowl is its commercials. While watching Super Bowl LX, hoping to see creative and humorous advertisements, I instead saw two commercials for Wegovy and Zepbound. Both commercials emphasized a single selling point: weight loss. Both companies are the main new competitors in the space of a revolutionary drug, GLP-1. This type of drug, GLP-1, is not a new thing; Ozempic has been around since 2017, but these drugs were initially advertised for type II diabetes, but have now since been used by celebrities and others for cosmetic weight loss. Although these drugs do help with weight loss, the other health benefits they provide should be what they focus on more, and the cost of these drugs are increasing due to the advertisement as a drug that can be used by anybody. These factors contribute to a GLP-1 revolution, but in the wrong direction.

Background

GLP-1 drugs (or agonists) are drugs that operate by mimicking the GLP-1 hormone, which is produced by the small intestine. It triggers insulin release, blocks glucagon secretion, and affects the part of the brain that makes you feel “full.” The first agonist to be approved by the FDA was in 2005, and since then many different companies have their own for different purposes.

Support

These drugs provide extraordinary gastro-intestinal health benefits, but they are not limited to just that. GLP-1 drugs have been prescribed for heart disease prevention, lowering blood pressure, and improving fatty liver disease. These other health benefits, along with the initial prescription for diabetes and blood sugar regulation, are deserving enough for GLP-1 drugs to be widely available to the public. Weight loss and the fight against obesity are also worthy problems these drugs attempt to battle, and they are effective. These benefits along with evidence of improved behavioral and metabolic changes, make it clear that the emergence of these drugs are beneficial to patients and clinicians due to their versatility and effectiveness.

Critiques

One of the main issues with GLP-1 drugs are some of the side effects, where even low doses causes extreme nausea, and extreme cases see malnutrition due to the loss of appetite and vomiting, though these are issues you can see with any drug. The main issue with these drugs is the companies that hold them. The advertising, and pricing of these drugs is where the issues lie. The high premiums, wide variety of patient coverage, and effective monopolist companies cause the high pricing which makes these beneficial drugs nearly impossible to afford for lower income and poorly insured individuals. The more pressing concern lies not in the pharmacology of the drugs, but in their commercialization. Aggressive advertising campaigns increasingly target broad audiences seeking weight loss, regardless of medical necessity. This messaging risks framing GLP-1 drugs as lifestyle enhancers rather than serious medical treatments. There have also been non FDA approved GLP-1 compounds advertised online, which poses a risk for people who want to use these drugs but cannot afford them, and thus leading to a search for alternatives. Further transparency is needed in the advertising to educate the general public on who truly needs these medicines, as well as the other health benefits they can provide. The pricing issues can only really be addressed by insurance companies themselves, by making coverage for these drugs better and cost less for the plans that these coverages are included in.

Conclusion

GLP-1 drugs represent a breakthrough in metabolic medicine. Their ability to treat diabetes, reduce cardiovascular risk, and combat obesity makes them revolutionary. However, the current cultural and commercial focus on cosmetic weight loss risks distorting their purpose and limiting equitable access. If the GLP-1 revolution continues to prioritize marketing over medical necessity, it may ultimately undermine the very patients these drugs were designed to help. A shift toward responsible advertising, improved insurance coverage, and better public education would ensure that this pharmaceutical advancement moves in the right direction.

  • Written by Noah Love, Content Writer at SPAN.
